title: What not to put on the site for a small consultancy
metaTitle: What to leave off a small consultancy site
excerpt: Cut the industry list. It reassures the team and tells a buyer they might as well do the work themselves. Keep the problem and a way to book a session.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it, a draft being marked up the way a long site should be cut.
caption: A long draft is ready when the extra lines are crossed out. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a small consultancy remove first?
faqs.answer: Remove the list of industries, including softer versions such as a claim that you work across sectors. It reads as range without a problem. Keep a setting only when it changes the work, inside the problem sentence or a single proof, not as a menu.

faqs.question: What should remain on the site?
faqs.answer: Keep the problem, the working session with its length and boundary, one proof of a decision the buyer would have delayed, and a way to book. Bios and fees can stay when they are specific. A vague page kept so the menu looks full is worse than no page.

faqs.question: How do you cut the page without a fight?
faqs.answer: Cover the phone screen after about ten seconds and ask what problem the firm takes. If the answer is only consulting, the first screen failed. Test each defended block by asking what true thing the buyer loses if it goes. Range is not that thing.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The most common small consultancy website mistakes start with a list of industries and a page that performs taste. The list reassures the team that no sector is excluded. It confuses a buyer who is comparing you with doing the work themselves. They already know their sector. A list tells them your method is generic, which is what they have in-house. Keep the problem you actually take and a clear way to book a working session. A shorter site that tells the truth will beat a long one that looks considered.

Nielsen Norman Group's account of attention is the limit. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. On the visits they make, they read only about a quarter of the words, and the average visit lasts a little less than a minute. Every extra block bets they will read past the problem. Most will not. Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether, after reading, someone knows enough to act, or whether they have to search again. A long page that never names the stuck decision sends them back to the work they were already doing.

## Cut the industry list first

The list is the mistake the firm defends, because it feels like honesty about range. Range is not the offer. The offer is a problem with an edge. "Healthcare, logistics, professional services, consumer, technology" is a tour. "We force the pricing decision a founder has been rewriting" is an offer. Delete the tour from the homepage, the navigation, the footer, and the form. If a setting changes the work, it can live inside one proof, as part of the constraint, not as a badge.

Do not replace the list with a softer list. "We work across sectors" is the same sentence with the nouns removed. Do not replace it with a map. A map is a list drawn as geography. The buyer does not need to see that you have been on a plane. They need to see that the session ends with a choice.

If a partner says a buyer will not recognize themselves without their industry, put the recognition in the problem sentence. "Pricing for a single-location firm that still quotes by phone" contains a setting because the setting is the constraint. It is not a menu. One setting inside the problem is specific. Six settings under the problem are the list again.

## The other performances of taste

Walk the site and mark anything a buyer could find on a firm they already decided not to hire.

A tasteful interior with no artifact. A values list. A five-step method in which every step is a meeting. A counter of clients. A carousel of logos with no decision attached. An origin story that does not change the session. A download that assigns homework. A navigation item called Insights that is not about the problem. A bio that says trusted advisor and does not name the work.

None of these is a moral failure. All of them spend the quarter of the page someone might read. The values list is the clearest. It reassures the authors. It does not predict the hour. A refusal does. "We will not end the session with six priorities." That sentence can stay. "We value rigor" cannot.

Google's people-first questions are a good edit. Does the page show first-hand experience of a problem, or only a category. Would the reader leave able to book, or still unsure what they would be buying. A page written to look like a consultancy, rather than to help someone stop postponing a decision, fails even when nobody mentioned search. Write for the person who might come directly and then go back to their own draft. The category word can appear once. Then get out of the way.

## What stays

Keep four things. The problem, in the complaint they already use. The session: length, what they leave with, who must attend, what it is not. One proof with a constraint, a decision, and a cost they would have delayed. A path to book, with a promise you can keep.

Who is in the room can stay if the bio names the problem and the verbs. The fee shape can stay if it says what they stop doing and what they still own. If either is vague, do not keep a vague version so the menu looks full. A missing page is cleaner than a page that says bespoke.

A newsletter can stay as a quiet link. It should not share the first screen with the session. Two equal doors tell this buyer you want an audience. They came for an hour with an end.

## How to cut without a fight

The fight is about loss. A partner likes the sector logos because a past client was proud. A designer likes the interior. A new hire wants a thought-leadership tab.

Make the cut with the page on a phone. Cover it after ten seconds. Ask what problem the firm takes and what they would book. If the answer is "consulting" and "a call," the covered material was not the issue. The first screen was. Uncover the rest only after that answer is right.

Give each defended block a test. If we delete this, what true thing does the buyer lose. If the answer is our range, ask whether range helps someone who might do the work themselves. It does not. It is the reason they hesitate. Keep the problem. Lose the range.

Write the removals where the next designer will see them. "No industry list. No client counter without a decision. No second button in the hero. No origin story unless it changes the booking." Otherwise the list returns in the next refresh, because it is the default in a template.

## Length, and the sentences that repeat the hero

A short site is a firm that chose. One or two problems with boundaries. Two proofs with decisions someone would have delayed. One fee shape. One session. An about page that names who is in the room. That is complete for this buyer.

Add a page when you have a new problem you will be hired for, with its own sentence and refusal. Do not add a page because a competitor has a resource center. The quarter-of-the-words limit means the resource center will not be read by the person deciding whether to book. It might be read later, by someone who already trusts you. Later is not a reason to put it above the problem.

If a paragraph repeats the hero in softer words, delete it. Repetition feels like emphasis in the firm. On the page it feels like padding. The visitor who stays past about half a minute, the point at which people may stay much longer, will notice the padding and discount the rest. Say the new fact or stop.

## A removal pass you can finish this week

Scroll the site once on a phone and mark five kinds of waste.

1. Any industry list, map, or "we work across" sentence.
2. Any number you cannot define in one clause.
3. Any heading that is a department or a sector rather than a problem or a decision.
4. Any sentence that could be pasted onto another firm's site unchanged.
5. Any second action that competes with the session.

Delete the marks. Do not replace them with something of equal length. The gap is the point. Then read the problem and the session to someone who has been doing the work themselves. If they can repeat both, and they can say why they would not simply continue alone, the site is shorter and truer. If they cannot, you deleted the sentence that was doing the work. Put that sentence back. Delete a different block.

Also search the site for the old sector names after the redesign. Leftover links and alt text will keep the list alive. Replace them or remove them. A site with two vocabularies will be believed in the vaguer one.

One more pass belongs to the pictures. If a frame is a lounge, a city, or a grid of workplaces, it is the industry list in pixels. Replace it with the artifact of the decision, or leave the space empty. Do not keep a handsome photograph because the page looks bare without it. Bare is readable. A buyer skimming on a phone will take the empty space as confidence and the collage as doubt. Doubt is what they already feel about hiring anyone. Do not illustrate it.

When this site tells the truth about one problem, a different kind of firm still needs a different first screen. Read [what the homepage has to prove for a creative studio](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-creative-studio) if the work you are describing is a studio's, not a retained decision in a room.

If you want that cut made with someone who will argue for the shorter page, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the industry list you are willing to delete. The hour is for what remains.
